lesson.title: Why a Capacitor's Opposition to Current Depends on Frequency
lesson.summary: Capacitive reactance measures how strongly a capacitor opposes AC current, and unlike resistance it shrinks as frequency rises because the capacitor has less time to charge before the current reverses.
lesson.body:
A resistor opposes current the same way regardless of how fast the voltage changes, but a capacitor behaves completely differently. A capacitor stores charge on its plates, and the current flowing into it is proportional to how quickly the voltage across it is changing, not to the voltage itself. At low frequencies, the voltage changes slowly, so relatively little current needs to flow to keep the capacitor charged to match it. At high frequencies, the voltage changes rapidly, demanding much more current to keep up. The practical result is that a capacitor's opposition to AC current, called capacitive reactance and given the symbol Xc, gets smaller as frequency increases, the opposite of how an opposition might intuitively be expected to behave.

The formula for capacitive reactance is Xc = 1 divided by (omega C), where omega is the angular frequency in radians per second and C is capacitance in farads, giving Xc units of ohms, exactly like resistance. Since omega = 2 pi f, this is equivalently written Xc = 1 divided by (2 pi f C). Notice both C and omega sit in the denominator, so doubling the capacitance halves the reactance, and doubling the frequency also halves the reactance. At the theoretical extreme of a DC signal, where f = 0, Xc becomes infinite, meaning a capacitor completely blocks DC current once fully charged, a fact you have likely already encountered when using capacitors to block DC while passing AC.

Worked example: take a 10 microfarad capacitor, C = 10 times 10 to the minus 6 farads, connected to a 60 Hz AC source. First find the angular frequency: omega = 2 pi f = 2 pi (60) = 376.99 rad/s. Then apply the reactance formula: Xc = 1 divided by (376.99 times 0.00001) = 1 divided by 0.0037699, approximately 265.26 ohms. Checking the arithmetic in stages: 376.99 multiplied by 0.00001 equals 0.0037699, and 1 divided by 0.0037699 gives approximately 265.26. So this capacitor presents about 265 ohms of opposition to a 60 Hz signal, noticeably more than the roughly 132.6 ohms it would present at 120 Hz, since doubling the frequency halves the reactance as the formula predicts.

This frequency dependent behavior is the working principle behind capacitors used in filters. A capacitor placed in series within a high pass filter offers high reactance at low frequencies, blocking them, and low reactance at high frequencies, passing them through easily. Placed in parallel instead, as in a simple low pass filter, that same falling reactance at high frequency gives high frequency signals an easy path to ground while leaving low frequency signals largely undisturbed. It is Xc's frequency dependence, not merely its existence, that makes frequency selective filtering possible at all.

It is important to keep reactance conceptually distinct from resistance even though both are measured in ohms. Resistance dissipates energy as heat, while reactance stores and releases energy without dissipating it, which is why reactance and resistance combine using complex number arithmetic, impedance Z = R + jXc, rather than simple addition, a distinction that becomes essential once resistors, capacitors, and inductors appear together in the same AC circuit.
